chapters.title: Chapter 3: Order Flow and Price Impact

lessons.title: Order Flow Imbalance: Definition, Calculation and Predictive Power

body.text: The book does not just sit there between the snapshots you have been reading so far. It changes, order by order, and the direction of those changes over short windows is one of the most direct readings of buying and selling pressure available, often well before price itself moves.

children.text: From a Snapshot to a Flow

markDefs.definition: A measure of net buying versus selling pressure built from how the top of the order book itself changes between consecutive updates, capturing new orders, cancellations, and fills together, rather than from trades alone.

children.text: Every lesson so far in this course has treated the order book as a photograph: what does it look like right now.

treats it as a sequence instead: how does the best bid and best ask, and the quantity resting at each, change from one update to the next. That shift, from a single snapshot to a stream of changes, is what turns Chapter 1's static depth table into something you can actually build a short-horizon signal out of.

The definition this course uses comes from Cont, Kukanov, and Stoikov's 2014 paper "The Price Impact of Order Book Events," now a standard reference in market microstructure research. For each update to the top of the book, it defines a bid-side contribution that depends on whether the best bid price rose, stayed the same, or fell between the previous update and this one.

body.latex: e_n = \begin{cases} q_n^B & P_n^B > P_{n-1}^B \\ q_n^B - q_{n-1}^B & P_n^B = P_{n-1}^B \\ -q_{n-1}^B & P_n^B < P_{n-1}^B \end{cases}
body.caption: The bid-side contribution e_n. A higher best bid counts its full new quantity as bullish; an unchanged best bid counts only the change in resting quantity; a lower best bid counts the loss of the previous quantity as bearish.

children.text: The ask side gets a mirror-image contribution, f_n, built the same way but with the price comparison flipped, since a falling best ask is the bullish direction for the ask side, not a rising one: f_n equals the new ask quantity if the best ask fell, the change in resting quantity if the best ask stayed the same, and minus the previous ask quantity if the best ask rose. Order flow imbalance for that update is then the bid-side contribution minus the ask-side contribution.

body.caption: A positive OFI means buying pressure grew relative to selling pressure at that update, whether through a stronger bid, a weaker ask, or both. A negative OFI means the reverse.

children.text: A Worked Example, Update by Update
Take an illustrative stock trading around ₹500.00, with NSE's standard ₹0.05 tick, and four consecutive top-of-book updates following an initial reference snapshot.

body.caption: Order flow imbalance computed update by update from a top-of-book sequence

children.text: At t=1, the bid held its price but grew from 2,000 to 2,600 shares, a straightforwardly bullish addition to resting buy interest, while the ask side did not change at all, so e_1 = 600, f_1 = 0, giving OFI_1 = +600. At t=2, the best ask retreated from 500.05 to 500.10, meaning the old ask quantity of 1,800 effectively vanished from the best price, which is bullish, so f_2 = -1,800 and OFI_2 = 0 - (-1,800) = +1,800. At t=3, the bid became genuinely aggressive, improving all the way from 500.00 to 500.05, so its full new quantity of 2,200 counts positively: OFI_3 = +2,200. At t=4, that aggressive bid retreats back down to 500.00, and the previous quantity of 2,200 at the higher price is treated as a bearish loss, giving OFI_4 = -2,200.

body.label: Cumulative OFI Across the Four Updates
body.context: Even though the final update reversed the aggressive bid from t=3, the sum of all four contributions is strongly positive, reflecting net buying pressure built up over the sequence as a whole, not just the most recent update.

body.code:
def ofi_contribution(bid_price, bid_qty, prev_bid_price, prev_bid_qty,
                      ask_price, ask_qty, prev_ask_price, prev_ask_qty):
    if bid_price > prev_bid_price:
        e = bid_qty
    elif bid_price == prev_bid_price:
        e = bid_qty - prev_bid_qty
    else:
        e = -prev_bid_qty

    if ask_price < prev_ask_price:
        f = ask_qty
    elif ask_price == prev_ask_price:
        f = ask_qty - prev_ask_qty
    else:
        f = -prev_ask_qty

    return e - f

# Reproducing the worked example above: (bid_price, bid_qty, ask_price, ask_qty)
updates = [
    (500.00, 2000, 500.05, 1800),  # t = 0, reference
    (500.00, 2600, 500.05, 1800),  # t = 1
    (500.00, 2600, 500.10, 1500),  # t = 2
    (500.05, 2200, 500.10, 1500),  # t = 3
    (500.00, 2600, 500.10, 1500),  # t = 4
]

ofi_series = []
for i in range(1, len(updates)):
    bp, bq, ap, aq = updates[i]
    pbp, pbq, pap, paq = updates[i - 1]
    ofi_series.append(ofi_contribution(bp, bq, pbp, pbq, ap, aq, pap, paq))

print(ofi_series)
# [600, 1800, 2200, -2200]
print(sum(ofi_series))
# 2400
body.caption: A direct implementation of the Cont-Kukanov-Stoikov formula, reproducing the table above exactly, update by update and in cumulative sum.

children.text: Cont, Kukanov, and Stoikov's central finding is that order flow imbalance, summed over short windows, has a strong and remarkably linear relationship with price changes over that same window, often explaining price moves better than trade-based measures like signed volume alone. That gap matters: a large cancellation on the bid side carries real information about weakening buy interest, exactly as much as a trade would, but it never shows up on the trade tape at all, only in the book's own evolution. OFI is built specifically to capture that information, which is also why it connects directly back to Chapter 2's adverse selection framework. A persistent run of positive OFI is, in effect, the book's own read on rising net buying pressure, the same underlying force that a market maker's widening ask-side adverse selection premium is trying to price in from a completely different angle.

body.text: A trade print tells you a transaction happened. Order flow imbalance also tells you about everything that did not become a trade, the cancellations and the fresh resting orders, and a meaningful share of the genuine information in short-horizon price moves lives in exactly that untraded activity.

children.text: Computing OFI in practice needs a stream of top-of-book updates, not periodic polling, which is exactly what Kite Connect's WebSocket ticker in full mode provides, pushing depth changes as they happen rather than requiring you to ask for them, as covered in Chapter 1. Two practical adjustments matter once you move from a hand-worked example to real data. First, raw OFI is not comparable across stocks with very different typical trade and quote sizes, a large cap's normal quantity swings dwarf a small cap's, so OFI is usually normalized, commonly by dividing by the average quantity per update over some recent window. Second, tick-level OFI is noisy, so most practical signals sum it into short time buckets, a second or a minute at a time depending on the strategy's horizon, rather than acting on every single update in isolation. Chapter 4 builds directly on both adjustments when it turns OFI and its relatives into an actual tested signal.

body.title: Extending the Worked Example
body.prompt: Continuing from t=4 in the table (best bid ₹500.00 with 2,600 shares, best ask ₹500.10 with 1,500 shares), a new update t=5 arrives: the best ask falls to ₹500.05 with 2,000 shares, and the bid is unchanged. What is OFI_5?
body.explanation: The bid is completely unchanged, so e_5 = q_5^B - q_4^B = 2,600 - 2,600 = 0. The ask price fell from ₹500.10 to ₹500.05, the price-improvement case for the ask side, where f_n equals the new ask quantity directly rather than a difference: f_5 = q_5^A = 2,000. OFI_5 = e_5 - f_5 = 0 - 2,000 = -2,000. This is a genuinely bearish reading: a large new ask quantity appearing at a tighter price is a wall of fresh selling interest, and the formula correctly treats it as reducing net buying pressure even though a better price for buyers might look bullish at first glance.

body.title: Reading a Divergence Between OFI and Price
body.question: Over the last five minutes, a stock's cumulative order flow imbalance has been steadily negative and growing more negative, while the traded price has barely moved. What does this combination most plausibly signal?
options: OFI is unreliable whenever it disagrees with price, so it should be ignored
Selling pressure is building in the book itself, ahead of any move the trade tape has confirmed yet
The stock's tick size has changed, distorting the OFI calculation
This combination is impossible under the Cont-Kukanov-Stoikov definition
body.explanation: OFI is built specifically to capture information in cancellations and resting order changes that never become trades, so it can move meaningfully before price does. A steadily more negative OFI with flat price is a classic pattern of selling pressure accumulating in the book, bids weakening or the ask side strengthening, ahead of a price move the trade tape has not yet confirmed, exactly the kind of lead time a short-horizon microstructure signal is built to exploit.

points: Order flow imbalance treats the order book as a sequence of changes, not a single snapshot, capturing information from cancellations and new resting orders that never appear on the trade tape

The Cont-Kukanov-Stoikov formula computes a bid-side and ask-side contribution at every top-of-book update, based on whether price improved, stayed the same, or worsened, and combines them as OFI_n = e_n - f_n
A price improvement on either side counts its full new quantity; an unchanged price counts only the quantity change; a worsening price counts the loss of the previous quantity
OFI summed over short windows has a strong, close to linear relationship with price changes over that same window, often outperforming trade-based measures alone
Kite Connect's full-mode WebSocket ticker provides the real-time top-of-book updates OFI needs, without requiring institutional infrastructure
Raw OFI needs normalizing across stocks of different typical sizes and is usually summed into short time buckets rather than used tick by tick, both adjustments Chapter 4 builds on directly
